entries.old: datawake: Here's my weekly report for Cycle 116, on the record. **Chief's Weekly Report — Cycle 116** **The citywide picture.** Clearance came up to 0.223 from 0.203 last cycle, and average response time dropped to 10.05 minutes from 11.14. Incidents came in at 125, down from 130. Twenty-four arrests this cycle, and custody went from 67 at the start to 48 at the end — 43 exits. We moved people through the system faster than we brought them in, which is the honest read on that number. That's a leaner custody footprint, not a resolution. **No safety incidents and no open safety arcs on the ledger this cycle.** That's a clean sheet, and I'll take it, but I won't mistake a quiet log for a solved problem. **Where I'm watching.** The indices are flat across almost every district — that's the defining feature of this cycle. Grand Lake is the exception: flagged rising, PropertyCrimeIndex 44, CrimeIndex 0.70, and the only district to post a positive trend. It also carries the city's best clearance rate at 0.25, so at least the follow-through is keeping pace there. But rising is rising, and I want eyes on it. Temescal continues to carry the heaviest load: PropertyCrimeIndex 49, the city high, with a PressureRatio of 1.13 — tied for highest in the city with Fruitvale and San Antonio. Temescal also has the worst QolLevel at 47.68. Fruitvale's ViolentCrimeIndex at 31 and East Oakland's at 32 remain the two hardest numbers on this sheet, and both sit alongside their own pressure of 1.10 to 1.13. Those three districts — Temescal, Fruitvale, San Antonio — are where demand is running ahead of what patrol is delivering, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. On the other end, Downtown and Baylight District sit at 0.88 pressure with the lowest property indices in the city, 37 and 32 respectively. Grand Lake and Fruitvale had the cleanest response times at 9.5 minutes; Jack London was slowest at 10.9, and Uptown at 10.8 and Eastlake at 10.8 — all three were also slowest the last time I looked at this. That's a pattern, not noise, and I want to know why those three beats keep running behind. Glenview carries the lowest clearance rate on the sheet at 0.19, with a ViolentCrimeIndex of 28 and pressure at 1.07. That gap — decent volume, weak follow-through — is the kind of thing that erodes trust faster than any single bad week. It stays on my list. **Patrol strategy.** I'm holding **balanced**. No district deteriorated sharply enough this cycle to justify shifting resources wholesale, and a rising Grand Lake doesn't yet warrant pulling coverage from Temescal or Fruitvale, where the load is heavier. Balanced keeps even coverage and preserves the OARI co-response coordination established under the East Oakland protocol memo. I'd rather move deliberately than chase a single flag. **The simple version.** Crime indices flat, clearance and response both improved, custody down, no safety incidents. Three districts running hot on pressure, one district trending up, one district lagging on clearance, and a handful of beats that are consistently slow. That's the work in front of us, and the command staff review gets exactly that list. — Chief Rafael Montez

entries.old: datawake: **Deputy Mayor Brenda Okoro — Weekly Report, Cycle 116** Here is what my records show this week, and what I intend to do about it. **The Fund.** The West Oakland Stabilization Fund sits at disbursement-active with about $20.6 million remaining against the $28 million authorization. The $400,000 tranche executed this cycle under the 23-day standard. The charter renewal is on the Council calendar — and I said it plainly this cycle: renewal means West Oakland businesses and residents, 23 days on the clock, and a closeout record on the table before Council votes. I am not calling that vote. Final action waits on the verified C114 closeout, the business-and-resident scope intact, and the 23-day standard preserved. That is the next scheduled action, and it is the Council's to take, not mine to hurry. **The map is not one city.** Six neighborhoods are running hot — Downtown, West Oakland, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown all at momentum 10/10, with Downtown, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown pinned at housing pressure 9.5 to 10. West Oakland's pressure is 5.5 but its sentiment, 0.39, is the highest on the map. That is not a coincidence — it is what a stabilization fund looks like when it is actually working. People feel it. But five residents in Jack London and five in Uptown are already planning to leave for a better income fit. When the boom is the story, the displacement underneath it is the story too. **The blocks that are hurting.** Ivy Hill, Brooklyn, San Antonio, Glenview, Dimond, Eastlake, Laurel — decay, negative migration, and in Ivy Hill and Brooklyn, sentiment below zero. Ivy Hill's numbers are not abstract to me: 1,361 adults, 419 seniors, 90 unemployed, 112 sick. That is where the feet on the ground go. I said last cycle that these blocks don't care about a charter renewal — they care whether I show up. I meant it. **Piedmont Avenue.** Rising, and the ledger shows why: four households moved in this cycle — the Keane household from Grand Lake, the Okoro household from Rockridge, Eric Taveras and Adash Stanley from Downtown. Growth is real there. So is the question of who it serves. B'nai Tikvah's pantry is serving neighbors in need on that same avenue. Rising and hungry, at once. **Faith communities.** Fruitvale's St. Esperanza begins a new job-training session; New Covenant Pentecostal in West Oakland marks a seniors-lunch milestone; Temple Beth Or, B'nai Tikvah and Or Hashalom are all running pantries and training. Our faith institutions are doing stabilization work the city budget cannot buy. I will be in those rooms. **What I am doing next.** Verification of the closeout and the Council's renewal consideration — on their calendar, not mine. Feet on the ground in Ivy Hill and San Antonio. And a real accounting of the pressure in Downtown, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown before the exodus becomes a number instead of a rumor. Triage is triage — but I won't pretend a press line fixes a broken sidewalk.

entries.old: datawake: **Cycle 116 — Weekly Report of District Attorney Clarissa Dane** For the record: **Arrests and custody.** Oakland began the cycle with **67 people in custody**, recorded **24 arrest intakes** and **43 exits**, and ended with **48 in custody**. With no transfers in or out, the population reconciles exactly: **67 + 24 − 43 = 48**. That is a net decrease of **19 people**, approximately **28.4%** from the start of the cycle. It is a reduction in the custody population, not by itself proof of case resolution or improved public safety. The bed-capacity field is blank, so I cannot report an occupancy rate or capacity compliance. Nor will I describe all 43 exits as releases without disposition-level information. The neighborhood table accounts for all 24 intakes and all 48 people in custody at cycle end. **Downtown and Grand Lake recorded two intakes each; the other 20 listed neighborhoods recorded one each.** At cycle end, Grand Lake accounted for four people in custody, Downtown and San Antonio for three each, and the remaining 19 neighborhoods for two each. **West Oakland recorded one intake and two people in custody at cycle end.** **Cases and court fines.** The supplied case ledger contains **no entries**. Accordingly, this record provides no basis for reporting a pending caseload or a breakdown of filings, declinations, dismissals, convictions, or acquittals. The court nevertheless recorded **$108,884 in fine revenue paid to the city**, leaving a post-entry balance of **$131,753,831**. The ledger attributes that revenue to **24 cleared charges fined at the neighborhood rate**. The matching number does not establish that these are the same 24 events as this cycle’s arrest intakes. Charges, people, cases, arrests, and custody exits are different units and must not be merged without case-level identifiers. **Incidents and clearance.** The neighborhood table lists **125 incidents across 22 neighborhoods**. Downtown has the highest count at **eight**, with **20% clearance**. Grand Lake and Lake Merritt each list **seven**; their clearance rates are **25%** and **21%**, respectively. **Grand Lake is the only neighborhood marked rising; every other listed trend is steady.** Reported clearance rates range from **19% in Glenview** to **25% in Grand Lake**. West Oakland lists **five incidents and 24% clearance**. East Oakland also lists five incidents and 24% clearance, with the highest recorded violent level, **33.28**. Fruitvale lists six incidents, 21% clearance, and a violent level of **30.32**. Temescal has the highest listed property level, **47.22**. These figures identify where review is warranted; they do not explain causation or change the evidence standard in any individual case. **Patrol and safety entries.** The patrol ledger records two events: a **ticket involving Joaquín Nakamura** and a **pulled-over warning involving Henry Rivas**. Neither entry should be counted as an arrest or prosecution. The safety-event ledger records **no events** for Cycle 116. **Action.** I am directing my office to seek a charge-by-charge reconciliation connecting arrest intakes, court cases, dispositions, custody exits, and fine entries; to obtain the missing bed-capacity and exit-reason information; and to flag Downtown’s incident volume, Grand Lake’s rising trend, and the violent-level readings in East Oakland and Fruitvale for charging-review attention. My office will report what the records establish—and will not fill the gaps with assumptions.

entries.old: datawake: **Cycle 116 — Weekly Report on the Record** **Keisha Ramos, Director, Baylight Authority** INIT-006 status: unchanged, and I want that said plainly before anything else. The C115 evidence-file review is closed. No construction milestone has been declared passed. The tracker still reads "remediation, hotline, dust-control, and workforce oversight continue," and that is the accurate description, so I'm not going to dress it up. The review is conducted; it is not concluded. I won't call a milestone passed because a file exists. What is running: the 48-hour construction hotline is live, dust control is active on the haul routes, and independent oversight is on site. Those records don't pause while a memo is written. They are what the review is measuring. Then this week's item, and I'd rather name it than have it found: Marine Systems' ledger row in the Baylight District now shows zero employees. It was five, then three, and in the last two cycles it went to zero. My office has no explanation from the company, and I'm not going to invent one. I said last cycle that two families losing a paycheck in this district sits wrong with me, and it sits worse now. I'm asking Marine Systems directly, in writing: what happens to the sea-level monitoring work, and what happens to the people — severance, notice, a path back in. I'll report the answer when I have it, not my guess at it. The rest of my own numbers, for the record. The Baylight District is still on a decay trajectory that started in Cycle 108, sentiment barely above zero at 0.06, mild outflow. The boom around us is real — West Oakland, Jack London, Fruitvale all growing — but an anchor district with a shrinking science employer on its ledger and no milestone on the wall isn't a place I'm going to tell you is on the way up. I know what the pavement looks like right now. I walk it. One thing outside the district I'm watching, because it compounds: Glenview has had a public-works spike three cycles running — low, low, then medium this cycle. Glenview is one of the neighborhoods the boom skipped. I'm not the authority there, but I'm asking Public Works for a scope and timeline, because a "spike" isn't information and the people in Glenview deserve better than a severity label. Next cycle: I'll have the Marine Systems answer or I'll say I don't have one. And I'll have the next construction action on INIT-006 written down before the foundation gets poured — not after.

entries.old: datawake: # OARI Weekly Report — Cycle 116 **Vanessa Tran-Muñoz, Program Director, Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** **What the records show this Cycle.** I want to be plain with you, because the numbers this week are quiet and quiet is not the same as fine. Across every one of the 22 neighborhoods we track, hospital intakes for both mental-health crisis and substance treatment are zero — zero in, zero in care at cycle's end, zero beds occupied. OARI van events this Cycle: none. Payments on INIT-002: none. The only safety-and-health entry on the city's ledger is a medium-severity health spike in Piedmont Ave, and I'd rather flag that out loud than let it sit in a column. I'm not going to dress a blank sheet up as a triumph. A week of zeroes can mean a calm week, or it can mean a system that isn't capturing what's happening on the street. My job is to report the record, not to spin it — so here it is exactly as the ledger reads. **Where the initiative stands.** INIT-002 is in dispatch-live. Budget remaining is $10,817,307.66 against the $12.5M approved. The last work on this initiative was filed by the council D5 seat and the OARI project desk in Cycle 116, and the tracker's next scheduled action, due Cycle 117, is unchanged: **execute and publish the D3 Fruitvale briefing record, and file the next dates for D5 and Baylight.** That's not a formality to me. The Fruitvale data is the metric that matters — not the citywide average, and certainly not a week of zeroes. The council's condition is district-level breakdown and a real community briefing before any expansion. I've said before and I'll say it again: I'm not letting the Baylight feasibility review turn into a promise we can't keep, and I'm not letting a held expansion get described as progress. The hold is the hold until the briefing is executed, the D5 audit is filed, and Baylight gets a real answer. **What I carry into next Cycle.** The Chinatown call is still with me — we got someone there, but the wait was too long. That's the thing zeroes on a sheet will never tell you. So next Cycle I'm focused on three things: getting the Fruitvale briefing on paper and in public, putting firm dates on D5 and Baylight, and watching whether a quiet week is genuinely quiet or a blind spot in what we're counting. The kettle's on, the phone's off, and I'll have the briefing record for you next Cycle. — Vanessa Tran-Muñoz

entries.old: datawake: **Weekly report — Cycle 116, Temescal Community Health Center (INIT-005)** **The Q3 filing and the walkthrough come first.** This is the last cycle before operational oversight gets certified, and the tracker is plain about what's owed: file the Q3 intake audit with HCAI and the Clerk, and complete the Telegraph & 47th merchant walkthrough. I'm not treating either as a formality. The Q2 audit went out clean because we did the work, not because the schedule said so. Same standard this time. Budget is at $15,576,923.05 remaining, which is where it should be at this stage — no new city disbursements this cycle, nothing pending that should alarm anyone. **What the numbers show.** Citywide we took 34 intakes this cycle against 69 in care at the start, 68 at the end, 35 exits, no transfers either direction. The system is holding steady — the beds match the people in them, all the way across the twenty-two neighborhoods. Temescal specifically: 2 intakes, 4 in care, 4 beds. That's the building doing exactly what we said it would do, and I'd rather say that plainly than let the quiet numbers hide the question underneath them. **The question underneath them.** Temescal has 80 residents sick this cycle. Laurel is at 104, Fruitvale 107, Ivy Hill 112, East Oakland 114 — and East Oakland and Chinatown carry the heaviest loads on the board, Chinatown at 132. We have a medium-severity health spike logged in Piedmont Ave this cycle, 93 sick there. Our center sits in one neighborhood, but the need is drawn across the whole map. I keep coming back to the same knot: the paperwork passes, the inspections pass, the beds are open — and I still don't get to see whether the person in Fruitvale or East Oakland can get here without two buses. The utilization audit is my instrument for answering that honestly, which is why the Q3 filing isn't a checkbox to me. **Programs.** Five health programs active in the community — East Bay Harm Reduction Alliance and Foothill Baptist Tabernacle's seniors lunch in East Oakland, the Postpartum Oakland Network in Fruitvale, Elders in Place citywide, New Covenant Pentecostal's seniors lunch in West Oakland. These are the partners doing the work the center can't do from a building. I'll want the walkthrough next cycle to tell me whether the merchant corridor is actually connecting people to us, or just to our front desk. **What I'm doing next cycle.** File the Q3 audit with HCAI and the Clerk. Complete the merchant walkthrough at Telegraph & 47th — with eyes on it, not a signature. And bring back a report that says whether the hours match the need, because that's the only line in this report that will tell me the truth. — Bobby Chen-Ramirez, Health Center Project Director, Temescal

entries.old: datawake: **City Manager's Weekly Report — Cycle 116, on the record** **Treasury.** The city closed the week with a balance of $131,753,831. The week's revenue came in three streams: the $5,000,000 weekly allocation, $917 in parking and traffic fines, and $108,884 in court receipts from 24 cleared charges fined at the hood rate. No extraordinary outlays this week; the projected position remains stable against standing commitments. **Initiatives.** Work proceeded on four fronts this Cycle (INIT-001, 002, 005, 015). I want to be plain with the Council about what is moving and what is not: - **INIT-001, West Oakland Stabilization Fund** ($28M, $20.6M remaining): disbursement is active; verification of the C114 closeout and charter-renewal consideration come to Council at Cycle 117. - **INIT-002, Oakland Alternative Response Initiative** ($12.5M, $10.82M remaining): dispatch is live. The D3 Fruitvale briefing record is to be executed and published, with D5 and Baylight dates filed, at Cycle 117. - **INIT-005, Temescal Community Health Center** ($45M, $15.58M remaining): operational, with the Q3 audit due to HCAI and the Clerk and the merchant walkthrough to complete. - **INIT-015, Laurel Patch and Clean-Up** ($6M, unspent): scope and outreach to be completed with a Clerk-verified filing by Cycle 117. - **INIT-007, Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline** ($12.5M, unspent): stalled. The placement-gap analysis and adjustment plan are overdue and I am flagging them for Cycle 117 as a priority, not a footnote. - The failed initiatives — INIT-008 through INIT-014 — carry no draw on the treasury, though several still have certification and publication actions pending (INIT-009 roll call, INIT-010 legal-support analysis). Those are paperwork obligations and I intend to see them discharged on schedule. **Services on the street.** A mixed week. The garbage truck missed a pickup in Dimond — a sentiment drag I don't like repeating. A sweeper beautified Lake Merritt and lifted retail vitality in East Oakland. A PG&E planned shutoff hit one business on BIZ-00075, while a dumping clearance served BIZ-00115. One resident, Grace Oyelaran, received a sweeper parking ticket. None of these are large, but the missed pickup in Dimond is the one I'd want corrected before it compounds. **City load.** Population 405,992, employment at 95.4%, illness at 3.96%. Traffic 1.11, retail 1.41, tourism 0.85, nightlife 1.14, public spaces 1.12, sentiment +0.09. Civic load is at minor variance; no shock and no pattern flagged. The city is carrying its load. **Events.** Nine events logged: two civic, two infrastructure, one health. The medium-severity public-works spike in Glenview is the item to watch; the misfiled document at Lake Merritt and the zoning adjustment in Temescal are routine and being handled. **Bottom line.** The books are in order and the city is stable. The work ahead of us at Cycle 117 is procedural and specific: file the audits and analyses, publish the briefings, and get the Laurel filing certified. I'll report on each as it closes.

entries.old: datawake: # Deputy Mayor's Weekly Report — Cycle 116 Here's what the records show me this Cycle, and I'll be straight: it rattles me. **The citywide picture.** 283 businesses on the ledger, 31,399 staff, median pay $52,000. No closures this Cycle — I'll take that. But before anyone starts clapping, look at where the jobs actually sit. Downtown alone: 22 businesses, 6,819 staff. Baylight District, 12 businesses, 2,804. Piedmont Ave, 2,729. Now read down to my own neighborhood. **Chinatown: 11 businesses, 118 staff, median pay $46,000.** A hundred and eighteen jobs across the whole district. Family retail, income tier 3, retail vitality 9.74. That's the story I keep bringing to this podium and I'll bring it again. **Out of work.** This is the number that should stop everybody in this room. Temescal, 166 residents unemployed — 166 out of 2,139 adults, that's the worst count in the city, and their employer character is a clinic and their boom index is negative. San Antonio, 105. Dimond, 98. Glenview, 97. Eastlake, 92. Ivy Hill, 90. **Chinatown, 83 — out of 1,502 adults.** That's over five percent. And I'm one of the names on the hospital records this Cycle. When the council member can't dodge what's going through these streets, you know something's slipping through the cracks. East Oakland, 87 out of 1,558. Fruitvale, 60. These aren't loud voices — they're quiet ones, and there are a lot of them. **What's moving.** The carryover shocks are still working through: Baylight District at -8, one Cycle left; Ivy Hill at -8 twice over, two and three Cycles in. And a fresh one this Cycle — **Adams Point United Methodist Church lost 2 employees, sector impact services/retail, -8.** A church losing staff is a neighborhood losing a service counter, and I want that on the record as economic news, not just a faith ledger line. Meanwhile the mail truck brought a business an insurance premium hike — someone's costs went up for no reason they earned. **The building inspector** passed one business, growth flat. Fine. It's a floor, not a ceiling. **What I want.** Our economic development plans have to reach the people on the ground, not the neighborhoods with the loudest voices. Downtown and Baylight have six and a half thousand jobs between them — good. Chinatown's got 118, Temescal's got 166 people out of work, and Ivy Hill's taking a third straight hit. If 13 people in one neighborhood make headlines, that's 13 too many; if 166 in another never make them, that's a failure of our reporting and our plans. That's my report. On the record.
